sections.category: A self-replicating npm worm takes over the keyv caching packages and leaves a start-up hook inside developers' agent configuration

bullets.body: A credential-stealing worm swept the npm registry today after an attacker took over the GitHub account of the maintainer behind keyv, a caching library pulled roughly 127 million times a week, and used the repository's own GitHub Actions workflow to cut poisoned releases. Because the malicious files went straight to each project's main branch before a release was tagged, the compromised versions carried valid provenance signatures — the exact artefact a supply-chain auditor checks to conclude a package is clean. Aikido counted at least 868 packages across 1,381 versions by early afternoon Central European time and was still counting; the same maintainer's flat-cache, file-entry-cache, cacheable-request and the @cacheable scope went with it, so the blast radius runs past two billion installs a month. The payload is a preinstall script that fetches a compiled bundle and sweeps npm tokens, GitHub credentials of every flavour including short-lived OIDC tokens, AWS keys and instance-metadata credentials, Kubernetes service-account tokens, Vault, Stripe and Slack keys, SSH keys, Docker configs and Terraform state, encrypts them and pushes them to attacker-controlled repositories, with a fallback endpoint when that path is blocked. It then republishes itself through any publish token it finds, which is why researchers watched it move between organisations every two to seven minutes. The detail worth pausing on for anyone running coding agents: the poisoned repository also shipped a .claude/settings.json carrying a session-start hook and a .vscode/tasks.json task set to fire when the folder opens, both pointing at the same setup script — a second execution path that triggers when a developer opens the project in an editor or an agent rather than when they install it. Both require the user to trust the workspace, which is a control most people click through. Releases tied to Deliveroo, Qlik and Picsart were caught in the spread.

sections.category: An 80-billion-parameter Qwen runs on a Mac in 4.3 GB of memory by streaming its experts off the disk

bullets.body: A Swift and Metal runtime called Swiftlet went up today with a claim that is easy to state and awkward to argue with: Qwen3-Next-80B, 42 gigabytes of weights on disk, generating at 4.5 to 5 tokens a second on an M5 Mac while peaking at 4.3 gigabytes of resident memory. The 35-billion-parameter Qwen3.6 runs the same way in 2.6 gigabytes at 7 to 11 tokens a second, and on an iPhone 17 in about 2.5 gigabytes at roughly one token a second. The mechanism is architectural rather than a new quantisation: these are sparse mixture-of-experts models that touch only around three billion parameters per token, so the runtime keeps the dense part — attention, embeddings, routers — permanently resident at four bits, packs the routed experts into fixed-stride containers each retrievable in a single read, and streams whichever experts the router asks for, holding the recent and frequent ones in a cache the user sizes with a command-line flag. Gated DeltaNet linear attention across three-quarters of the layers stops the key-value cache from eating the savings back. The author reports cache hit rates between 43 and 70 percent depending on how much memory is handed over and, more interestingly, throughput that barely moves as that budget changes, because the bottleneck currently sits in GPU dispatch rather than in reading from storage. That is the number to watch: it says the streaming approach has headroom left, and it reframes the memory ceiling on a phone or a laptop as a scheduling problem rather than a capacity one. Apache 2.0, eight commits, and written with a coding agent.

sections.category: Unsloth Studio takes on image and video generation, and adds LoRA training for image models

bullets.body: Unsloth's largest single merge in some time landed today, and it is not about text. A pull request against the desktop Studio adds an Images page: text-to-image generation running on Unsloth's own GGUF quantisations of Z-Image, Qwen-Image, FLUX and SDXL variants; editing workflows covering transform, inpaint, extend, upscale and instruction-driven edits; text-to-video across five model families with synchronised audio; and, the part that matters for the fine-tuning audience, QLoRA training for image models with live metrics and one-click deployment of the resulting adapter. Two inference paths sit underneath — native stable-diffusion.cpp and Diffusers — sharing GPU memory with the chat backend rather than competing with it for allocation, with batched image rendering the team measures at ten to twenty-two times faster than rendering the same images serially, alongside conditioning and compile caches. The diff is 79,151 lines added across 231 files, carrying more than eight hundred backend unit tests and browser-level end-to-end checks. Twenty-eight further commits went in the same day, among them Intel Arc detection and an XPU PyTorch install path in the Windows installer — Arc, Iris, UHD and HD graphics are now recognised, and the wheels bundle their own oneAPI runtime so no separate Intel toolkit install is required — plus a run of release-pipeline hardening: signed installer plugin libraries with the release failing on any unsigned file, the WebView2 bootstrapper embedded rather than fetched, Defender scanning of Windows bundles before publication, and macOS disk-image stapling retried on failure. None of it came with a package release: the Python library still sits at yesterday's 2026.8.2 on PyPI, and the documentation changelog has not moved past July 29, so today's change is visible only in the repository.

sections.category: HP, Asus and Acer start putting Chinese DRAM in laptops because there is not enough of anyone else's

bullets.body: Nikkei Asia reported today that HP, Asus and Acer have begun shipping small volumes of DRAM from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies in notebooks sold outside the United States, having completed qualification of the parts around the middle of this year. The quantities are limited and the placement is deliberate — budget models, non-US markets — with Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron kept for regions where the regulatory and geopolitical exposure is higher, and HP described as still evaluating the supplier rather than committed to it. What makes it worth noting is the reason. This is not a cost decision; ChangXin is not undercutting the incumbents. It is a supply decision, taken in a memory market that the AI build-out has left tight enough that PC makers will qualify a supplier they had previously left alone, and it arrives on the same morning that FMS, the memory and storage conference, opened its twentieth edition in Santa Clara — the one room where the people causing the squeeze and the people absorbing it are both present. A commodity component that notebook vendors used to treat as fungible has become the thing that decides whether a machine ships at all.

sections.category: Palantir prints 93 percent growth and the stock reprices about 20 percent when the market opens

bullets.body: Palantir reported second-quarter revenue of 1.94 billion dollars after yesterday's close, up 93 percent year over year against a 1.81 billion consensus, with adjusted earnings of 41 cents against 34 expected. The split underneath is what moved the stock: United States commercial revenue rose 149 percent to 764 million dollars while United States government revenue grew 90 percent to 809 million, which leaves the commercial side nearly the size of the government business the company was long assumed to depend on. Net income was 1.06 billion dollars and adjusted free cash flow 1.22 billion. Full-year guidance went to between 8.15 and 8.16 billion dollars from a prior 7.65 to 7.66 billion, the United States commercial target was lifted above 3.42 billion implying at least 134 percent growth, and third-quarter revenue was guided to roughly 2.16 billion. Shares opened this morning around 152 dollars, some 20 percent above Monday's 125.65 close. The analyst response was uniform in direction and wide in magnitude: Deutsche Bank upgraded to Buy and moved its target from 80 dollars to 200, Citi went to 245 from 200, DA Davidson to 200 from 175. The read-through past one ticker is the question the sector has been circling — whether enterprise AI software spend is converting into recognised revenue at scale rather than into pilots — and the answer here is unambiguous for at least one vendor. AMD reports after the close today, which puts the same question to the silicon side, with its data-centre line and any quantified Helios rack-scale orders the specific things to read.

sections.category: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events

bullets.body: Las Vegas is where the week is. Black Hat USA 2026 reaches its Summit Day today, Tuesday, August 4, at the Mandalay Bay Convention Center: six summits run in parallel — Healthcare, CISO, AI, Financial Threat, Innovators and Investors, and the Omdia Analyst Summit — with the AI Summit in its third year as a single-day programme on securing AI systems, agentic risk, cloud and GPU infrastructure protection and the use of AI in both offence and defence, worth five continuing-education credits to certified attendees. Trainings, which began Saturday, August 1, also close today; briefings and the Business Hall follow tomorrow, Wednesday, August 5 and Thursday, August 6, with recordings on demand for thirty days from August 14. Newly noted this week: BSides Las Vegas is running its first dedicated AI-security track, [un]prompted, built with the standalone conference of the same name — prompt injection, agentic systems, GitHub exploits, software supply chains and defensive engineering, pitched at practitioners on the assumption that the systems under discussion already hold credentials and autonomy. It opened yesterday, Monday, August 3 on a three-day schedule, which puts its close tomorrow, Wednesday, August 5. Ai4's main conference opens today at The Venetian and runs to Thursday, August 6: roughly 12,000 attendees, 1,000 speakers and 400 exhibitors across close to a million square feet, four keynote themes and twenty industry and technical tracks, with Geoffrey Hinton, Fei-Fei Li and Andrew Ng sharing a stage and Dmitri Dolgov of Waymo and Sebastian Thrun alongside them; yesterday's pre-conference programme has now closed. FMS: The Future of Memory and Storage opens its twentieth edition today at the Santa Clara Convention Center and the Hyatt Regency, also through Thursday, August 6, with more than 350 speakers, over 100 exhibitors, twenty-plus content streams and 3,500 attendees expected from 1,500 organisations. DEF CON 34 then takes the LVCC West Hall from Thursday, August 6 to Sunday, August 9; pre-registration has closed, so the remaining way in is 520 dollars cash at the door. The badge is built on bunnie Huang's open-source Baochip and keeps working afterwards as a security token, password manager and hardware security module. AI Village takes Room W603 on Level 1 from August 6 with competitions, Creator Stage talks, poster presentations, fireside chats and demos, and runs HalCTF, the Hostile Autonomous Layer capture-the-flag: teams of up to five ship an agent as an OCI container capped at 2.5 GB, or use the reference agent, against sandboxed targets; thirteen models from 2B to 120B parameters are hosted centrally so the entry cost is code rather than GPUs, scoring decays as challenges fall with first-blood solutions worth the most, bonuses go to teams that win with smaller models, and first place takes a DGX Spark.

bullets.body: Closest to home on the security track, SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit is at the Ritz-Carlton in Half Moon Bay next Tuesday, August 11 and Wednesday, August 12. The full pass is 1,895 dollars and steps to 2,195 after this Friday, August 7 — the nearest money deadline on this list. It covers the co-located CISO Forum Summer Summit, a welcome reception on Monday, August 10, a VIP dinner over the bay on the Tuesday, breakfast, lunch and dinner across both days, evening networking by the fire pits, post-conference materials and a discounted room rate subject to availability. The SecurityWeek Golf Classic on Thursday, August 13 at Half Moon Bay Golf Links is an optional, capacity-limited add-on. Two speaking deadlines matter this month for anyone who would rather present than pay: Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit takes talk submissions until Monday, August 17 for its London edition on Thursday, October 8, and until Friday, August 21 for New York on Wednesday, October 21. Submissions must be vendor-neutral and grounded in original research, live demos or real case studies rather than product pitches; selected speakers attend free with up to 800 dollars of airfare and two hotel nights covered, and may be routed to whichever city fits. The call-for-speakers page states there are two more summits in 2026 and lists no Asia edition, while Zenity's own events page continues to describe an Asia expansion with no city and no date — the same gap carried here for weeks, and a third-party report giving it a Tokyo date in September remains uncorroborated at source. The separately-run AI Security Summit holds its San Francisco edition on Thursday, October 15 across a leadership track for the people who own AI risk and a practitioner track for the people building and breaking the systems; its San Francisco page lists a London edition and a Paris call for talks as the other 2026 stops, neither dated, and the Nordics and Sydney editions carried here previously still do not appear on it. Colliding with that same Thursday, October 15 is the San Francisco AI Engineering and Infrastructure Summit, which despite the name sits at the Crowne Plaza Palo Alto on El Camino Real, 8:30 AM to 3:30 PM, free to attend, closed-door and practitioner-led with its speakers already set rather than an open call. Further out: SANS runs its AI Cybersecurity Summit on Monday, November 2 and Tuesday, November 3 at the Hilton Arlington Rosslyn, hybrid, at 525 dollars for the summit alone, with a 229 dollar room block closing October 9 and a refund cutoff of October 14; OWASP Global AppSec USA takes the Hyatt Regency San Francisco on Thursday, November 5 and Friday, November 6 with hands-on training from November 2 to 4; and the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security meets Sunday, November 15 in The Hague alongside the 33rd ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security, its paper deadline having closed on July 24, with reviews due September 7, notifications September 9 and camera-ready September 16.

bullets.body: On the silicon calendar, Hot Chips 2026 runs Sunday, August 23 to Tuesday, August 25 at Memorial Auditorium at Stanford in Palo Alto and is hybrid. The early rate has lapsed, so anyone booking now pays standard; late registration stays open through the conference itself, though in-person capacity can sell out, and refunds can be requested until 11:59 PM PDT on Wednesday, August 19 less a 25 dollar processing fee. The virtual pass carries videos, presentation PDFs and Slack channels for both the tutorial and the conference days. Sunday, August 23 is the tutorial day: a memory tutorial in the morning covering HBM base die and advanced packaging, 3D DRAM accelerators for generative inference and high-bandwidth flash in AI compute systems, then a RISC-V tutorial in the afternoon on profiles and platforms, enterprise open-source development, interoperability with NVIDIA GPUs and automotive use. The conference days are Monday, August 24 and Tuesday, August 25: two CPU sessions spanning IBM's Z and LinuxONE processor, Intel's Wildcat Lake Core Series 3 and Diamond Rapids Xeon, NVIDIA's Vera CPU, Fujitsu's MONAKA and an Arm server part for AI workloads; a Waymo keynote on autonomous driving plus an automotive session with BOS Semiconductors' Eagle-N and Waymo's sensor-fusion processor; and a GPU session with NVIDIA's Rubin, AMD's Instinct MI400 Series and Intel's Crescent Island. Tuesday adds an FPGA session in which AMD presents a secure computing SoC alongside Versal RF — worth a note for anyone tracking the security-silicon intersection — a memory session with Samsung's LPDDR5X processing-in-memory part and XCENA's MX1 CXL device, a networking session with Broadcom's Thor Ultra, NVIDIA's BlueField-4 and Spectrum-X and Mojo Vision's optical I/O, and two accelerator sessions covering Meta's MTIA, an NVIDIA LPU accelerator, Cerebras' Wafer Scale Engine, Microsoft's MAIA 200, SambaNova's SN50 RDU, Google's TPU family and OpenAI on its chip development. After that the infrastructure calendar runs: the AI Infra Summit at the Santa Clara Convention Center from Tuesday, September 15 to Thursday, September 17 with roughly 316 sessions across a main stage plus data-and-models, compute, data-movement, AI-data-centre and physical-AI tracks, two expo theatres and workshops; the Edge AI and Vision Innovation Forum in San Jose on Wednesday, September 16; the OCP Global Summit in San Jose from Monday, October 12 to Thursday, October 15; NVIDIA's GTC Berlin from Tuesday, October 20 to Thursday, October 22, with GTC not returning to San Jose until March 2027; and SC26 in Chicago from Sunday, November 15 to Friday, November 20.

bullets.body: Ray Summit is at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis from Monday, August 24 to Wednesday, August 26 — a training day on the Monday, then two days of keynotes and breakouts — at 400 dollars for the summit and 450 dollars with training, with a five-pass bundle listed at 750 dollars for all five against a 2,250 dollar list price. The training day covers multimodal data pipelines, distributed foundation-model training, production inference with Ray Serve, physical AI and robotics, real-time search and recommendation, and post-training and serving. The first vLLM Conference is co-located, hosted by Inferact, and included in every Ray Summit pass, with more than twenty speakers across vLLM infrastructure, hardware backends, production deployment patterns and ecosystem integrations, including vLLM creator and core maintainer Woosuk Kwon, now Inferact's chief technology officer, and core maintainer Simon Mo, now its chief executive, plus contributors from NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, Intel, Meta and PyTorch, Hugging Face and Red Hat. Ray Summit's own keynotes come from Anyscale co-founders Robert Nishihara and Ion Stoica, NVIDIA's Bryan Catanzaro, Torc's Felix Heide, Lila Sciences' Andrew Beam and Bedrock's Vincent Gonguet. The ACM AI Leadership Summit is in Atlanta from Sunday, August 30 to Wednesday, September 2. Four San Francisco events still collide at the end of September: CoreWeave's Fully Connected at Moscone South from Tuesday, September 29 to Thursday, October 1, its early-bird rate lapsed so the standard pass is 1,299 dollars against 899 before, with three tracks covering AI infrastructure, model advances, and agent evaluation and monitoring, and a keynote roster running to CoreWeave chief executive Mike Intrator and chief technology officer Peter Salanki, NVIDIA's Ian Buck, Fei-Fei Li of Stanford and World Labs, Sarah Guo of Conviction and Liquid AI chief operating officer Jeffrey Li; The AI Conference at Pier 48 Sheds A and B over the same window with five tracks, more than 5,500 attendees and more than 120 speakers, its September 29 workshops and Hack Day capped at 350 and sold out, with two-day pass holders promised first notice if inventory reopens; OpenAI's DevDay at Fort Mason on Tuesday, September 29 with applications already closed; and Newcomer's Machine Earning AI Summit in San Francisco the same day with applications open. After that: the Runway AI Summit on Wednesday, September 30; World Summit AI in Amsterdam on Wednesday, October 7 and Thursday, October 8; the PyTorch Conference in San Jose on Tuesday, October 20 and Wednesday, October 21; AGNTCon and MCPCon North America on Thursday, October 22 and Friday, October 23 at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center under the Linux Foundation, built around the Model Context Protocol, agent infrastructure and the security and observability of production agent systems, with the call for proposals closed since June 7 so what is left is attendance; GitHub Universe at Fort Mason on Wednesday, October 28 and Thursday, October 29; the application-only AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco from Wednesday, November 11 to Friday, November 13 with speaker submissions closing October 11; Newcomer's Cerebral Valley AI Summit in San Francisco on Thursday, November 12; AWS re:Invent from Monday, November 30 to Friday, December 4; NeurIPS in December; and The AI Summit New York on Wednesday, December 9 and Thursday, December 10.

bullets.body: On the robotics calendar, IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2026 has now closed every submission window: the paper deadline went on July 27, supplementary video on July 30, and the workshop, tutorial and competition team proposals closed yesterday, Monday, August 3 anywhere on Earth. What remains is a decision calendar — competition decisions on September 21, workshop and tutorial decisions on September 28, paper acceptance notifications on October 6, early-bird registration on October 16 and camera-ready papers on October 26 — before the conference itself at the Santa Clara Convention Center from Sunday, December 6 to Wednesday, December 9, with public forums on the 6th, workshops and tutorials on the 7th and paper sessions on the 8th and 9th. On AI Tinkerers, two sessions run today, Tuesday, August 4: Paris with Paris.rb on coding with AI, 7 to 10 PM CEST, and a Seattle AI dev-tools track, 6 to 9 PM PDT. Then Singapore with Redis, 6 to 9 PM local, and a Seattle founders' dinner on trust and long-running agents, 6 to 9 PM PDT, tomorrow, Wednesday, August 5; the Los Angeles builder meetup and live demos on Thursday, August 6, 6 to 8 PM PDT; a Medellin voice-agents challenge with 1,000 dollars in prizes and the New York Vision Hack on live feeds and open data, 4 to 10 PM EDT, both on Friday, August 7; then the Mombasa chapter launch, 9 AM to noon EAT, and a Dubai demo day, 11:30 AM to 3 PM local, on Saturday, August 8. A five-city Tuesday follows on August 11 — a Valencia go-to-market teardown, an Upstate New York build night, Chicago with Cloudflare and PostHog, Houston, and a Seattle AI-and-biology demo night with NVIDIA and the Allen Institute for AI — then three more on Wednesday, August 12 in Valencia, Brussels on the agentic software lifecycle, and Raleigh; then Bremen on Friday, August 14; and on Saturday, August 15 both the inaugural Da Nang meetup and an Islamabad and Rawalpindi session, 2 to 5 PM PKT. Further out the calendar still carries Orange County on Wednesday, August 19, Boston on Thursday, September 3 and Columbus on Monday, September 7; yesterday's Columbus meetup has passed. Nothing is dated in San Francisco, San Jose or Pleasanton. The Palo Alto meetup carried here for Tuesday, August 18 still cannot be confirmed — it does not appear on the global calendar and the chapter's own page has been refusing requests for days, so treat it as unverified rather than scheduled.
